issue.issue_text: Whether the failure to put each material circumstance appearing in the evidence to the accused during their examination under Section 313 of the CrPC amounts to a serious irregularity that can vitiate the trial.

facts: The appellant was convicted for serious offenses, including murder.
The conviction was based on a single piece of incriminating evidence: a witness (PW5) testified that the appellant was standing outside the crime scene with a 'katta' (a firearm) in his hand.
This specific and crucial circumstance was not put to the appellant during his examination under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC).
law: Section 313 of the CrPC requires the court to question an accused person about every material circumstance that appears in the evidence against them.
The purpose of this examination is to give the accused an opportunity to explain the evidence.
Failure to put a material circumstance to the accused is considered a serious irregularity.
This irregularity will vitiate (invalidate) the trial if it is shown to have caused prejudice to the accused, resulting in a failure of justice.
application: The Court determined that the witness's statement about the appellant holding a 'katta' was the only piece of evidence linking him to the crime.
By not questioning the appellant about this specific circumstance, the trial court denied him the opportunity to explain it.
Since the appellant's conviction was based solely on this unexplained circumstance, the Court found that the omission caused him serious prejudice.
This prejudice amounted to a failure of justice, as the conviction was based on evidence the appellant was never given a chance to address directly.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the failure to put the only material incriminating circumstance to the accused during his Section 313 examination was a serious irregularity that caused him prejudice. Therefore, the trial was vitiated, and the Court set aside the appellant's conviction and sentence.

issue.issue_text: Whether it is just to remand a case to the Trial Court for recording a further statement of the accused under Section 313 of the CrPC to cure a procedural defect, especially after a significant passage of time (over 27 years) since the incident.

facts: A procedural defect occurred during the trial where the only incriminating evidence against the appellant was not put to him during his statement under Section 313 of the CrPC.
Over 27 years had passed since the date of the incident.
The appellant had already been incarcerated for a period of 10 years and 4 months.
law: Section 313 of the CrPC requires the court to question an accused to enable them to explain any circumstances appearing in the evidence against them.
Failure to put a material circumstance to the accused is a serious irregularity that can vitiate the trial if it causes prejudice.
In some cases, such a defect is curable, and an appellate court can remand the case to the trial court to record a further statement from the accused.
When deciding whether to remand a case to cure such a defect, the court must consider the passage of time since the incident.
application: The Court acknowledged that while remanding a case is a possible remedy for a curable defect, it questioned whether it would be just to do so in this specific instance.
The primary reason against remand was the extreme passage of time. The Court stated that it would be unjust to ask the appellant to explain a circumstance that transpired 27 years ago.
As a secondary but persuasive factor, the Court noted that the appellant had already served a significant prison sentence of over 10 years.
Considering these two factors together—the long delay and the time already served—the Court concluded that the option of remand would be unjust.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the option of remanding the case. It held that due to the extreme passage of time (27 years) and the substantial period of incarceration already served by the appellant, it would be unjust to send the case back to the trial court to cure the procedural defect. Consequently, the Court found that the conviction was vitiated by the irregularity and set aside the appellant's conviction and sentence.

appellant_arguments: The only material circumstance appearing against the appellant in the evidence was not put to him during his statement under Section 313 of the CrPC.
The questions posed to the appellant were such that any person of ordinary intelligence would get the impression that no prosecution witness had stated anything against him.
The failure to question the accused on each material circumstance is a serious procedural irregularity, as Section 313 casts a duty on the court to do so to enable the accused to explain.
The appellant had specifically raised this contention in written submissions before the High Court, but the argument was not considered.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: It is the duty of the Trial Court to put each material circumstance appearing in the evidence against the accused specifically, distinctively and separately. The material circumstance means the circumstance or the material on the basis of which the prosecution seeks the conviction of the accused.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The failure of the Trial Court to put each material circumstance appearing in the evidence to the accused specifically, distinctly, and separately during their examination under Section 313 of the CrPC amounts to a serious irregularity. This is because Section 313 casts a duty on the court to question the accused for the express purpose of enabling them to explain any circumstances appearing in the evidence against them. Consequently, a court must ordinarily eschew from consideration any material circumstances that were not put to the accused.
legal_tests_applied: It is the duty of the Trial Court to put each material circumstance appearing in the evidence against the accused specifically, distinctively and separately. The material circumstance means the circumstance or the material on the basis of which the prosecution is seeking his conviction.

Section 313 of the Code casts a duty on the court to put in an enquiry or trial questions to the accused for the purpose of enabling him to explain any of the circumstances appearing in the evidence against him.
The Court must ordinarily eschew material circumstances not put to the accused from consideration while dealing with the case of the particular accused.
If any irregularity in putting the material circumstance to the accused does not result in failure of justice, it becomes a curable defect.
policy_considerations: The procedural safeguard in Section 313 of the CrPC is based on the principle of fairness, ensuring that an accused person is given an opportunity to explain any incriminating evidence before it is used against them.

It is unjust to remand a case to cure a procedural defect, such as an improper Section 313 examination, after an inordinate and significant passage of time (in this case, over 27 years) since the incident.
